stimulus.text: George Washington, Farewell Address, published September 19, 1796: “It is our true policy to steer clear of permanent alliances with any portion of the foreign world.” Washington also warned, in the most solemn manner, against “the baneful effects of the spirit of party generally,” saying it “serves always to distract the public councils and enfeeble the public administration.” The address was published in a Philadelphia newspaper, not delivered as a speech, as Washington left office after two terms.
stimulus.source_note: George Washington, Farewell Address, published September 19, 1796. Public domain.

source: original; stimulus quotes George Washington, Farewell Address, published September 19, 1796, public domain.
stem: Washington’s warnings in the Farewell Address most directly reflected which division of the 1790s?

options.text: The division between the North and the South over the spread of slavery.
options.misconception: The address warns about parties and foreign ties, not about slavery’s spread.

options.text: The division between settlers and American Indians over western land.
options.misconception: The address warns about parties and foreign ties, not about western land.

options.text: The division between supporters of a strong navy and supporters of a large army.
options.misconception: The address warns about parties and foreign ties, not about the navy and army.

options.text: The division between Federalists and Democratic-Republicans over France and Great Britain.

rationales.D: Background: Federalists leaned toward Britain and Democratic-Republicans toward France, and each side accused the other of serving a foreign power.
rationales.A: The address warns about parties and foreign ties, not about slavery’s spread.
rationales.B: The address warns about parties and foreign ties, not about western land.
rationales.C: The address warns about parties and foreign ties, not about the navy and army.
rationales.general:
1. Washington warns against permanent alliances and against the spirit of party in the same address.
2. Background: Federalists leaned toward Britain and Democratic-Republicans toward France, and each side accused the other of serving a foreign power.
3. His two warnings are really one: foreign attachments were feeding party hatred at home.
4. So the address reflects the Federalist and Democratic-Republican split over France and Britain.
Remember: when two warnings sit side by side, ask how they feed each other.
